name: The four elements and geometric atomism
plain_explanation: Earth, air, fire, and water are not truly basic; underneath them are two kinds of right-angled triangle, which combine to build the faces of geometric solids -- and each element is really a tiny regular solid: earth is cubes, fire is tetrahedra, air is octahedra, and water is icosahedra.
precise_definition: Timaeus's theory that the four sensible elements are composed, at a deeper level, of two types of right triangle (half-square and half-equilateral), which combine into the faces of four of the five regular (Platonic) solids, with each element identified with a particular solid; the fifth solid, the dodecahedron, cannot be built from these triangles and is instead associated by Plato with the universe as a whole.
why_it_mattered: It is an early, if fanciful, attempt at mathematical atomism -- explaining physical qualities through underlying geometric structure -- and Russell treats the proportional relations among the elements as among the parts of the dialogue 'to be taken quite seriously.'
historical_origin: Draws on the theory of the five regular solids, recently completed in Plato's own day by Theaetetus (also set out in Euclid Book XIII).
examples: Atoms of earth are cubes; of fire, tetrahedra; of air, octahedra; of water, icosahedra.
Fire is to air as air is to water as water is to earth (continued proportion).
objections: The dodecahedron, having pentagonal rather than triangular faces, cannot be constructed from Plato's two basic triangles, so it is left out of the four-element scheme; Plato says only, obscurely, that God 'used' it 'in the delineation of the universe.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: The Pythagorean pentagram, linked here to the dodecahedron's pentagonal faces, was used by the Pythagoreans as a symbol of recognition, called 'Health.'
